papers.authors: Dušan Vukadinović, H. N. Smitha, Andreas Lagg, Sami K. Solanki, Juan Carlos Trelles Arjona
papers.abstract: Atomic parameters are a key ingredient for the synthesis of spectral lines to model observed spectra and to extract meaningful physical information about the observed astrophysical object. We use quiet-sun observations to test the reliability of the atomic parameter inference from observed spectra. Our focus is on the transition probability of spectral lines, denoted as log(gf). We apply a spectropolarimetric inversion method to quiet-sun disc-centre observations at 1.56 $μ$m from the GRIS/GREGOR spectrograph. We use the coupled method implemented in the globin inversion code, where atomic parameters are spatially coupled, and a single value of these parameters is determined for every spectral line over the entire field of view. We carry out tests to determine the sensitivity of the inferred log(gf) values to various atmospheric parameters and the data reduction fallibility. We find that our log(gf) values are weaker by 0.023 dex compared to the most recent study. This is most probably caused by the constraint imposed on the log(gf) parameter due to the spatial coupling, lifting the degeneracy between temperature and log(gf). We use the Markov chain Monte Carlo method to determine the uncertainty in the inferred log(gf) values. For the strongest lines in the spectral region, the uncertainty in log(gf) is 1-4 %, increasing to 12 % for weaker and blended lines. Our tests suggest that the log(gf) values inferred using the coupled method from globin are robust against any local contamination to the observed line profiles, such as spectral stray light, and return a reliable and unique set of log(gf) values for the strongest lines irrespective of the chosen atmospheric model and observation dataset. This result is valid as long as the underlying assumptions of line formation under local thermodynamic equilibrium and the completeness of the line list are satisfied.

papers.title: Electron processing of glycine: evidence for peptide-forming condensation reactions
papers.authors: A. T. Hopkinson, D. V. Mifsud, P. Herczku, Z. Juhász, B. Sulik, N. J. Mason, N. C. Jones, S. V. Hoffmann, A. Cassidy, L. Hornekær, S. Ioppolo
papers.abstract: The discovery of amino acids on asteroids, including samples returned from asteroid Bennu, and the detection of glycine on comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko support the hypothesis that glycine can form in extraterrestrial environments. Laboratory experiments show that glycine can form through both energetic and non-energetic processing of interstellar ice analogues. In the interstellar medium, glycine is exposed to various forms of energetic processing, including cosmic rays and the secondary electrons they generate, which have been shown to produce complex organic molecules, including peptides. This work investigates whether peptide-forming chemistry is a general consequence of energetic processing. Films of glycine and glycine-d3 were grown in two ultrahigh-vacuum chambers and irradiated with 1-2 keV electrons. The irradiated samples were subsequently characterised using infrared spectroscopy, temperature-programmed desorption, and vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy. Peptide formation through condensation reactions would produce water as a secondary product, and spectra obtained following irradiation of glycine-d3 showed evidence of D2O formation, supported by TPD measurements, which revealed H2O formation for glycine and H2O, HDO, and D2O for glycine-d3. VUV spectra of irradiated glycine showed the formation of decomposition products, including CO and CO2, as well as H2O. Following heating, a non-volatile residue remained on the surface. Electron irradiation of glycine produces reaction products similar to proton irradiation, suggesting that the resulting chemistry is not strongly dependent on the energy source. These findings support the possibility that larger organic molecules can form in a wide range of extraterrestrial environments. Such molecules may subsequently be incorporated into small bodies and delivered to planetary surfaces, potentially contributing to the emergence of life.

papers.title: Robust Measurements of the Cosmic Microwave Background Lensing Power Spectrum in the Presence of Anisotropic Cosmic Birefringence
papers.authors: Rui Zhou, Michael Doohan, Christian L. Reichardt
papers.abstract: Achieving the scientific potential of upcoming high-sensitivity cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization surveys requires lensing analyses that are robust to unmodeled distortions of the polarization field. One such possible distortion is anisotropic cosmic birefringence, a direction-dependent rotation of the linear polarization plane that may arise from parity-violating physics such as axion-like fields. We quantify the impact of both modeled and unmodeled anisotropic birefringence on the CMB lensing measurement in the Marginal Unbiased Score Expansion (MUSE) framework. Considering noise levels expected for current and future CMB surveys, we find that neglecting birefringence produces a positive bias in the lensing bandpowers that increases towards small angular scales. For a scale-invariant birefringence power spectrum $L(L+1)C_L^{αα}/2π=10^{-5}\,{\rm rad}^2$, the positive fractional bias can reach $(10.1\pm1.1)\%$ of the lensing power at $1375<L<2000$. Jointly estimating lensing and birefringence in the MUSE framework recovers the input lensing bandpowers and birefringence amplitude without detectable bias across all tested configurations. The joint MUSE estimator also reduces the scatter of the recovered birefringence amplitude by factors of $1.6\pm0.2$ to $2.4\pm0.3$ relative to a joint quadratic estimator, with the largest gains in the highest signal-to-noise configurations. These results indicate that a joint-field reconstruction with MUSE can recover unbiased estimates of the lensing and birefringence power spectra while still improving precision relative to quadratic estimators.

papers.title: Nonlinear models of Mira variables with long secondary periods
papers.authors: Yu. A. Fadeyev
papers.abstract: Calculations of nonlinear radial oscillations in asymptotic giant branch stars with an initial mass of $M_\mathrm{ZAMS}=1.6M_\odot$ were performed for initial helium and metal abundances of $Y=0.28$ and $Z=0.006$, respectively. Several models from the evolutionary sequence after the 4th thermal pulse were used as initial conditions for the hydrodynamic equations describing stellar pulsations with long secondary periods. Using the discrete Fourier transform of the hydrodynamic solutions we show that long secondary periods appear in Mira variables pulsating simultaneously in the fundamental mode and first overtone with non-multiple periods. The relative deviation from multiplicity is $δ_\mathrmΠ\le 1.2\times 10^{-2}$ and is responsible for mode splitting into equally spaced frequency components, each of which is a standing wave with a free outer boundary. The cycle length of long secondary periods is nearly 20 times that of the fundamental mode. Long secondary periodicity is a nonlinear effect that arises after reaching the limiting amplitude and develops over several hundred fundamental mode periods.

papers.title: Jupiter's Evolving Interior as a Source of Episodic Heating on Europa
papers.authors: Jasmine Sun, Benjamin Idini, Ruth Murray-Clay
papers.abstract: Jupiter's evolving interior can affect the orbital evolution of its moons through frequency-dependent tidal dissipation. We investigate how encounters between the Galilean satellites and Jupiter's oscillation modes affect the stability of the Laplace resonance and Europa's tidal heating. Using the N-body integrator REBOUNDx, we simulate the dynamical orbital evolution of Io, Europa, and Ganymede, with tidal migration timescales derived from three representative models of Jupiter's interior. Encounters with a Jovian tidal resonance can alter the libration state of the Laplace angle, excite orbital eccentricity, and/or destroy the Laplace resonant chain. The outcome of the satellite system depends on which moon experiences enhanced tidal migration. Resonance locks involving Io or Europa can sustain outward migration of the Laplace resonant chain, whereas Ganymede locks destroy the chain. Notably, transient resonance crossings can excite Europa's eccentricity without breaking the Laplace resonance. Under our adopted eccentricity-damping prescription, the baseline tidal power is typically of the order $10^{11}$-$10^{12}$ W, with transient episodes reaching roughly an order of magnitude higher power. These results provide a mechanism for episodic tidal heating on Europa without requiring thermal feedback within the satellites.

papers.title: Thermal evolution of Uranus and Neptune, hydrogen-water phase separation and the role of methane
papers.authors: Marina Cano Amoros, Nicola Tosi, Nadine Nettelmann
papers.abstract: Adiabatic evolution models of Uranus and Neptune with constant compositional stratification miss their observed luminosities: Uranus is fainter than commonly predicted, while improved equations of state (EoS) have recently led to a brightness problem for Neptune. In adiabatic models of Jupiter and Saturn, helium rain is thought to enhance luminosity. In the ice giants, hydrogen-water phase separation (H2-H2O demixing) with water rain has recently been predicted. We aim to understand how H2-H2O demixing and the EoS of water influence the luminosity of Uranus and Neptune. We use state-of-the-art EoS of H, He, H2O, and the H2-H2O phase diagram to build adiabatic three-layer models of the present-day structure that match the observed gravity field and the phase diagram. We compute evolution tracks with and without demixing, and for Neptune, with and without latent heat and methane, for which we provide an updated large-scale EoS including entropy. Without demixing, adiabatic Neptune with the revised AQUA EoS, without methane or latent heat, cools to its observed luminosity within 4.5 Gyr, in good agreement with the age of the Solar system. Applying the same assumptions to Uranus would require a Bond albedo of 0.43 to explain its luminosity. With demixing, the radii expand while the luminosity decreases. For Uranus, demixing leads to an equilibrium evolution with the incident flux that naturally explains its faintness. Demixing also makes Neptune fainter. Methane reduces the radius expansion but not the faintness problem. Favored Neptune models include demixing and methane at an initial C/O ratio of $\sim$1 due to CO ice accretion, with cooling times of $\lesssim 4 Gyr. Neptune requires an additional heat source unless its structure is primordial and the outer envelope is ice-poor, while hydrogen-water phase separation is an option to explain the structure and faintness of Uranus.

papers.title: Quiet-Sun magnetic field configuration inferred from the ratio of longitudinal fields measured in the Fe I λ6301 and λ6302 Å lines
papers.authors: Sergey Grigoryevich Mozharovsky
papers.abstract: The estimate of the longitudinal magnetic field obtained from the Hinode spectropolarimeter data will be different if it is determined in different ways. In particular, the values obtained by the Center Of Gravity (COG) method for the Fe I $λ$ 6301 and 6302 $Å$ lines do not coincide. Some of the differences are due to the different inaccuracies of the COG method for each of the two lines. However, some of the differences can be explained by the fact that the response functions of these lines to changes in the magnetic field are formed at different heights. This should be accompanied by a certain morphological structure of magnetic fields. It consists in the fact that most of the magnetic configurations of the quiet photosphere are similar to each other. To a rough approximation, their structure can be compared with the structure of a sunspot - there is a central region with the strongest field, close to vertical, and slopes - an analog of penumbra, where the field weakens and / or turns to horizontal. This turn occurs at the heights of the greatest response of the Fe I $λ$ 6301 and 6302 $Å$ lines to changes in the magnetic field with a turn length of about tens of kilometers.
